newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Trouble looms as Lesotho's rivals wrestle anew.
newsitem.headline: Trouble looms as Lesotho's rivals wrestle anew.

text.p: Dark clouds gathering over Lesotho politics threaten to bring down a deluge of violence on the country, analysts said on Tuesday.
Local observers fear a violent struggle ahead of elections scheduled for next year, drawing in the security forces which have proved incapable of staying out of politics.
For decades the pastoral kingdom the size of Belgium has seen repeated fighting and intervention by the military and royalty in daily politics.

Now Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle, facing divisions in his ruling Basutholand Congress Party (BCP), has left to form a new party, claiming to take a majority with him and the right to keep charge of parliament.

"There will be no change in the running of government since I still enjoy majority support of members of the national assembly," he told reporters in the capital after announcing his new party on Monday.
But Western diplomats said it was doubtful the move was valid, or that the government could effectively govern a country where unemployment runs at about 45 percent.
"It is a most unusual situation and nobody knows if Mokhehle's move was permissible in terms of the constitution," said one diplomat.
Lawrence Keketso, editor of the local Mopheme newspaper, said Mokhehle's move had been accompanied by violence, and much more was possible.
"This weekend, houses have been burnt and two people are dead in an incident that can be directly linked to the split. We might see more of such things," he told Reuters.
"There is no way the police and army can stay out of this. The security forces are highly politicised and they will be split between the two groups," he added.
Earlier this year the army was sent in to put down a police mutiny in Maseru, which resulted in a gunbattle.
Antoinette Handley, of South Africa's independent Institute of International Relations, said Lesotho's security forces were notoriously unreliable.
"The Lesotho security forces have no sense of coherence and they have no loyalty to the state. A close watch has to be kept on rogue elements in the security forces," she said.
Observers said the latest political wrangling had baffled the mountain kingdom's two million citizens.
"The move has caused more confusion than understanding and the only answer to the present constitutional confusion will be found in elections next year," Keketso said.
Handley said the country's neighbours and other states in the region which have twisted arms in Maseru in the past, might now press for early elections.
"That is what South Africa and the Southern African Development Community might push for behind the scenes, to let the electorate sort the matter out," she said.
Lesotho receives over half of its income from tariffs raised by the Southern African Customs Union and another 40 percent from money sent home by migrant workers in South African mines.
Any political instability was unlikely to have much effect on the economy, the analysts agreed.
The kingdom imports 90 percent of its needs and the maloti currency is pegged to the South African rand.
It has little to export except water, a precious commodity which brings in about $55 million a year from South Africa's industrial heartland.
Mokhehle's stated reason for walking out of the ruling party was that he believed his deputy and rival Malopho Qhobela had hijacked the BCP.
"The weekend's events have merely reinforced the notion that Lesotho is riddled with unstable and immature politics," said Handley.
